title: IP addressing, subnets, NAT, DHCP, ARP
scopeHtml: Scope: IPv4/IPv6, CIDR subnet math, NAT, DHCP, ARP with worked numbers. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What an IP address is
notes.html:
An IP address is a number that says which network a machine is on and which machine it is inside that network. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits written as four bytes: 192.168.1.23. That gives 2^32 = about 4.29 billion addresses, which ran out long ago (IANA's free pool ended in 2011).

An address has two parts: a network part (like the street) and a host part (like the house number). Where the split is comes from the subnet mask or prefix length.

192.168.1.23   = 11000000.10101000.00000001.00010111
mask /24       = 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000
network part   = 192.168.1      host part = .23

Industry examples. AWS charges for public IPv4 addresses since February 2024 (about $0.005 per hour per address), a direct sign of IPv4 scarcity. Google, Meta and mobile carriers (T-Mobile, Jio) are heavily IPv6.

Everyday analogy. A phone number: country/area code identifies the region (network), the remaining digits identify the subscriber (host).

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking an IP identifies a device forever. It is a current location in the network and changes with DHCP and moves.
  • Saying "IPv4 has 4 billion addresses so it is fine". Most are reserved or allocated.

notes.title: Private, public and special ranges
notes.html:
Some ranges are reserved for private use and are never routed on the internet (RFC 1918). Everyone reuses them, which is why your home and office both use 192.168.x.x.

Range CIDR Size Typical use
10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 10.0.0.0/8 16.7M big companies, AWS VPCs
172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 172.16.0.0/12 1.05M Docker default (172.17.0.0/16)
192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255 192.168.0.0/16 65,536 home routers
127.0.0.0/8 loopback localhost = 127.0.0.1
169.254.0.0/16 link-local "DHCP failed" self-assigned; also cloud metadata 169.254.169.254
100.64.0.0/10 CGNAT 4.2M ISP-level NAT, Tailscale
224.0.0.0/4 multicast mDNS, routing protocols

Worked example. Two companies both use 10.0.0.0/16 for their VPCs and later want to peer them. Overlapping ranges cannot be routed between, so one must be renumbered. That is painful, so plan CIDRs before creating VPCs (a one-way door in practice).

Industry examples. Android devices that show 169.254.x.x failed DHCP. Kubernetes commonly uses 10.244.0.0/16 for pods and 10.96.0.0/12 for services; clashes with a corporate VPN range are a classic outage.

Everyday analogy. Internal extension numbers in an office: ext. 101 exists in every company, meaningless outside.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that cloud metadata endpoints live in link-local space (the SSRF target).
  • Picking tiny VPC CIDRs (/24) and running out of IPs for pods.

notes.title: CIDR and subnet math
notes.html:
CIDR notation a.b.c.d/n means the first n bits are the network. Host bits = 32 - n. Addresses = 2^(32-n). Usable hosts = 2^(32-n) - 2 (network address and broadcast are reserved in classic subnets; AWS reserves 5 per subnet).

Prefix Mask Addresses Usable
/8 255.0.0.0 16,777,216 16,777,214
/16 255.255.0.0 65,536 65,534
/24 255.255.255.0 256 254
/26 255.255.255.192 64 62
/28 255.255.255.240 16 14
/30 255.255.255.252 4 2 (point-to-point)
/32 255.255.255.255 1 a single host

Worked example 1: which network is 10.1.5.77/26 in? /26 means block size 64 in the last octet (256 - 192). Blocks: 0, 64, 128, 192. 77 falls in 64 to 127. So network = 10.1.5.64, broadcast = 10.1.5.127, usable = 10.1.5.65 to 10.1.5.126 (62 hosts).

Worked example 2: split 192.168.10.0/24 into 4 equal subnets. Need 2 extra bits so /26: 192.168.10.0/26, .64/26, .128/26, .192/26, each 62 usable hosts.

Worked example 3: size a subnet for 500 hosts. 2^9 = 512 minus 2 = 510 usable, so 9 host bits, prefix = 32 - 9 = /23.

Worked example 4: do 10.0.0.5 and 10.0.3.9 share a /22 ? /22 = block size 4 in the third octet: 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.3.255. Yes, same network.

# Quick checks
python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; n=i.ip_network('10.1.5.77/26',strict=False); print(n, n.network_address, n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses)"
# 10.1.5.64/26 10.1.5.64 10.1.5.127 64
ipcalc 10.1.5.77/26

Decision gravity. CIDR design for a VPC: a /16 for the VPC, /20 subnets per AZ and tier. Easy to start, but VPC primary CIDRs cannot be shrunk and renumbering is a one-way door; secondary CIDRs can be added later in AWS. Alternatives: IPv6 (no scarcity), or overlay networks.

Industry examples. AWS EKS with the default VPC CNI gives every pod a VPC IP, which can exhaust /24 subnets fast; teams add secondary CIDRs or use prefix delegation. Supernetting (route aggregation) lets an ISP advertise one /16 instead of 256 /24s, which keeps the global BGP table at roughly 1 million IPv4 routes instead of far more.

Everyday analogy. Cutting a chocolate bar: each extra bit in the prefix cuts every piece in half.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the minus 2 (and minus 5 on AWS).
  • Not being able to convert /26 to a mask or block size quickly; practise 256 minus last mask octet.
  • Mixing up "/24 has 254 hosts" with "256".

notes.title: IPv6
notes.html:
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (2^128, about 3.4 x 10^38), written in hex groups: 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334. :: replaces one run of zero groups. A typical subnet is a /64 (the standard LAN size), a customer gets a /48 or /56.

Key differences: no NAT needed (every device can have a public address, firewalls do the protection), no broadcast (uses multicast), no ARP (uses Neighbor Discovery over ICMPv6), SLAAC lets a host build its own address from the router's advertised prefix, and the IP header has no checksum and is fixed at 40 bytes. Routers do not fragment; only the sender does (Path MTU Discovery is essential).

$ ip -6 addr show eth0
inet6 2001:db8:abcd:12:5054:ff:fe12:3456/64 scope global dynamic
inet6 fe80::5054:ff:fe12:3456/64 scope link

fe80::/10 is link-local, always present, used for neighbor discovery.

Worked example. One /64 holds 2^64 = 1.8 x 10^19 addresses; one home with a /56 has 256 subnets of that. Scanning a /64 at a million probes/s would take over half a million years, so address scanning is not a viable attack.

Industry examples. Google measures IPv6 usage at around 45 to 50 percent of its users (confirm current figure). Reliance Jio is mostly IPv6 and Meta's data centers are IPv6-only internally. Apple requires apps to work on IPv6-only networks (DNS64/NAT64).

Decision gravity. Dual stack is safe and reversible; IPv6-only internally saves NAT and address headaches but needs every dependency to support it.

Everyday analogy. Postal codes that never run out, so you never share a house number.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying IPv6 removes the need for a firewall. It removes NAT, not security needs.
  • Forgetting that "no NAT" does not mean "no privacy"; privacy extensions randomise addresses.

notes.title: NAT
notes.html:
Network Address Translation lets many private devices share one public IP. The NAT router rewrites source IP and port on the way out, remembers the mapping in a table, and reverses it for replies. The common form is PAT (port address translation): IP + port, so ~64,000 simultaneous flows per public IP per destination.

Outbound:  192.168.1.23:51234 -> 93.184.216.34:443
After NAT: 203.0.113.7:40001  -> 93.184.216.34:443
Table:     203.0.113.7:40001  <->  192.168.1.23:51234  (TCP, idle timeout e.g. 300 s)

Consequences: inbound connections from outside have no mapping so they are dropped (accidental firewall); peer-to-peer needs tricks (STUN, TURN, hole punching, UPnP); long idle connections get their mapping dropped silently, so keepalives matter.

Worked example (incident). An app talks to a database through a cloud NAT gateway with 1 public IP. 1,000 pods each open 100 connections to the same destination IP:port: 100,000 flows but only ~64,500 ports per (public IP, destination IP, port, protocol). Result: ErrorPortAllocation (AWS NAT gateway metric, 55,000 simultaneous per destination per IP is the documented ballpark; confirm in docs). Fix: more NAT IPs, connection pooling, or VPC endpoints.

Types. Source NAT (SNAT, outbound), destination NAT (DNAT / port forwarding, inbound), and 1:1 NAT (AWS Elastic IP mapping to an instance). Carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT) puts a second NAT inside the ISP, so many households share one public IP.

# Linux iptables SNAT/masquerade and port forward
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.1.0/24 -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DNAT --to 192.168.1.50:80
conntrack -L | head      # the NAT/state table

Industry examples. AWS NAT Gateway (billed per hour plus about $0.045 per GB processed in us-east-1; a famous hidden cost), Kubernetes kube-proxy using iptables/conntrack for Services, WebRTC apps using STUN/TURN servers (coturn).

Decision gravity. NAT is a cheap fix for address shortage but breaks end-to-end connectivity and adds a stateful bottleneck. Alternatives: IPv6, or PrivateLink / VPC endpoints for AWS service traffic. Adding it is reversible; relying on one NAT per VPC creates a single point of failure (use one per AZ).

Everyday analogy. A hotel reception: guests call out through the single hotel number, and reception remembers which room asked, routing the reply back.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing NAT is a security feature. It is a side effect, not a firewall.
  • Ignoring conntrack table exhaustion (nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet in dmesg).
  • Forgetting UDP flows also need mapping and have shorter timeouts.

notes.title: DHCP
notes.html:
DHCP hands a new device its network settings automatically. A client with no address broadcasts to the whole LAN; a DHCP server (often your router) answers with an offer. The famous four steps are DORA:

  1. Discover: client broadcasts from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 (UDP 68 to 67) "any server out there?"
  2. Offer: server proposes IP, mask, gateway, DNS, lease time.
  3. Request: client broadcasts "I accept that one" (so other servers withdraw).
  4. Acknowledge: server confirms; lease starts.

A lease (say 24 h) is renewed at 50% (T1, unicast to the same server) and at 87.5% (T2, broadcast). Across subnets a DHCP relay (the router's ip helper-address) forwards broadcasts to a central server.

$ sudo dhclient -v eth0
DHCPDISCOVER on eth0 to 255.255.255.255 port 67
DHCPOFFER of 192.168.1.23 from 192.168.1.1
DHCPREQUEST for 192.168.1.23 on eth0 to 255.255.255.255
DHCPACK of 192.168.1.23 from 192.168.1.1 -- renewal in 41893 seconds

Worked example. Pool 192.168.1.100 to .200 = 101 addresses. A cafe with 150 customers over a day and a 24 h lease runs out; shorten the lease to 1 h for guest Wi-Fi.

Industry examples. Kubernetes does not use DHCP for pods (CNI plugins allocate). Cloud VMs get addresses via DHCP from the hypervisor, but the cloud controls assignment. ISC Kea replaced ISC dhcpd; dnsmasq is common in homes.

Decision gravity. Static IPs for servers and infrastructure, DHCP reservations (fixed lease by MAC) for printers: reversible. Security: rogue DHCP servers can hand out evil gateways; switches use DHCP snooping.

Everyday analogy. Checking into a hotel: you arrive with nothing, reception hands you a room (IP), the wifi password, and a checkout time (lease).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying DHCP uses TCP. It is UDP ports 67/68.
  • Forgetting that DHCP failure leaves you with 169.254.x.x on many OSes.

notes.title: ARP
notes.html:
ARP finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address on the same LAN. Ethernet frames need a MAC; IP is only the destination in the packet. The sender broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.1? tell 192.168.1.23", and the owner replies with its MAC; the answer is cached (typically for tens of seconds to minutes).

For off-subnet destinations the host ARPs for the gateway, not the far server.

$ ip neigh show
192.168.1.1 dev wlan0 lladdr a4:2b:b0:11:22:33 REACHABLE
192.168.1.40 dev wlan0 lladdr 3c:22:fb:aa:bb:cc STALE

$ sudo tcpdump -i wlan0 -nn arp
ARP, Request who-has 192.168.1.1 tell 192.168.1.23, length 28
ARP, Reply 192.168.1.1 is-at a4:2b:b0:11:22:33, length 28

Security note. ARP has no authentication. In ARP spoofing an attacker answers "192.168.1.1 is at my MAC", becoming man-in-the-middle. Defences: dynamic ARP inspection on switches, static entries, and TLS above. A gratuitous ARP (a host announcing itself) is used legitimately for failover: Keepalived/VRRP moves a virtual IP and sends it so switches and neighbours update.

Worked example. Failover takes 3 s mostly waiting for ARP caches (some devices cache 60 s). Sending gratuitous ARPs on takeover cuts it to under 1 s.

Industry examples. Kubernetes MetalLB in layer 2 mode announces service IPs through ARP/NDP; AWS replaced ARP in VPC with a mapping service (no broadcast in the cloud network). Large flat L2 networks suffer from ARP storms, which is a reason to route at the rack (L3 to the top-of-rack switch) in modern data centers.

Everyday analogy. Shouting in a room "who is Priya?" and she raises her hand; you remember her seat.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking ARP crosses routers. It is local to one broadcast domain.
  • Not knowing IPv6 replaces ARP with Neighbor Discovery.

notes.title: Putting it together: an off-subnet request
notes.html:
Worked example with every address. Laptop 192.168.1.23/24, gateway 192.168.1.1 (MAC aa:aa), destination 93.184.216.34.

  1. Is the destination in 192.168.1.0/24? No, so the next hop is the gateway.
  2. ARP for 192.168.1.1, get MAC aa:aa.
  3. Build the frame: dst MAC aa:aa, src MAC (laptop); packet: src 192.168.1.23, dst 93.184.216.34.
  4. The router NATs the source to 203.0.113.7:40001 and forwards to the ISP; the frame is rebuilt with the ISP router's MAC.
  5. Reply returns to 203.0.113.7:40001, the router reverse-maps it to 192.168.1.23:51234.
ip route get 93.184.216.34       # shows via 192.168.1.1 dev wlan0 src 192.168.1.23

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the destination MAC is the final server's. It is the next hop's MAC.
  • Forgetting that the destination IP never changes across routers (except by NAT), but MACs change at every hop.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• IPv4 is 32 bits (4.3B addresses, exhausted); IPv6 is 128 bits, /64 per LAN, no NAT or ARP.
  • Private ranges: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16; plan VPC CIDRs early because renumbering is painful.
  • Subnet math: hosts = 2^(32-n) - 2; block size = 256 minus the mask octet; /24 = 254, /26 = 62, /28 = 14, /30 = 2.
  • NAT (PAT) shares one public IP by rewriting ports; watch port exhaustion, conntrack limits, and idle timeouts.
  • DHCP = DORA over UDP 67/68, with leases and relays; ARP maps next-hop IP to MAC on the local LAN.
  • Destination IP stays end to end; MAC addresses change every hop.
